plan.analysis: Only the constant solution exists (R=2/3 ≈ 0.6667). Theory suggests smooth, bell-shaped profiles should beat it: an exact Gaussian gives R=1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.7071, so the immediate target is the 0.70+ region. The main uncertainty is the optimal tail/peak shape, so I will spend one experiment on a parametric super-Gaussian family, one on a compact-support power bump, and one on direct coordinate ascent over the step heights to squeeze out shape improvements beyond any fixed parametric family. All start from p0001 but construct their own initial profile.

experiments.hypothesis: A smooth super-Gaussian h(x)=exp(-(|x-0.5|/s)^p) can exceed the constant 2/3; the Gaussian case p=2 should already give about 0.7071, and nearby p may do slightly better by flattening the top or changing tails.
experiments.change: Construct N=4001 symmetric heights on [0,1] using h_i=exp(-(|x_i-0.5|/s)^p). Do a coarse grid over s in logspace(0.03,0.5,25) and p in {1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0,4.0,6.0}, evaluate exact R from np.convolve(h,h), then refine the best (s,p) with scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead') maximizing R, using the remaining CPU time. Return the best heights found.
experiments.prediction: Best R will be in [0.700,0.712], strictly above 0.6667, with optimal p near 2 (or slightly above) and s around 0.12-0.18.

experiments.hypothesis: A compact-support bump may outperform a Gaussian-like bump because it removes slowly decaying tails that add to ||f*f||_1 without helping the peak; the family h=(1-|2x-1|^q)^p provides flat tops and variable edge behavior.
experiments.change: Construct N=4001 symmetric heights h_i=(1-|2x_i-1|^q)^p for |2x_i-1|<=1 and 0 otherwise. Grid q in {1.0,1.5,2.0,3.0,4.0} and p in {0.25,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,3.0,5.0}; evaluate exact R for each, then locally refine the best (q,p) with Nelder-Mead for the remaining budget. Return the best profile.
experiments.prediction: Best R will be in [0.698,0.714]; it may beat the super-Gaussian if a flatter top with compact support is favored, otherwise it will confirm that Gaussian-like tails are better.

experiments.hypothesis: Direct local search over individual step heights can find a better shape than any fixed parametric family, because the exact R objective can be optimized coordinatewise while preserving symmetry.
experiments.change: Use N=300 (or 401) symmetric heights; initialize with a super-Gaussian found by a quick internal sweep over s,p (or a constant if that fails). Then repeatedly sweep the free symmetric indices i=0..N/2-1: for each index try multiplying h_i by factors (1+eps) and (1-eps) for eps in a decreasing schedule (0.2,0.1,0.05,0.02,0.01,0.003,0.001), accept a change if exact R improves, and continue sweeps until the CPU budget is nearly exhausted. Use multiple random/parametric restarts only if time remains. Return the best R profile.
experiments.prediction: Coordinate ascent will improve on the best parametric result by at least 0.001-0.005, reaching R≈0.708-0.718, and will show that the optimal profile is a smooth symmetric bump slightly flatter than a Gaussian.

plan.analysis: p0002 (0.8122) is the only real breakthrough: strongly asymmetric (f*f max at 0.273, height ratio 4.67), while every symmetric family caps at ~0.724. Critically, p0002 used only 1.96 s of 20 s and was resolution-limited (N=800 from a 50-step start), so there is obvious unfinished business: everything inside its basin can still be polished. Its f*f is very peaked (only 8.2% of knots within 1% of max), so flattening the peak of f*f is the most plausible mechanism for more gain, since R is maximized when f*f is box-like. I bet on one strong refine (exact-gradient L-BFGS with full budget), one objective-relaxation idea (soft-inf annealing to deliberately flatten f*f), and one multistart test of whether better basins exist.

experiments.hypothesis: p0002 stopped after 1.96 s with crude random-block perturbation; it is inside a good basin but far from its local optimum. Exact analytic gradient + L-BFGS-B with nonnegativity, run for the full 20 s at higher resolution (N=2000 then 4000), will push R well past 0.812.
experiments.change: Take start (p0002's 800-step profile), resample by linear interpolation to N=2000, normalize mass. Implement _R (as in p0002) plus its exact gradient w.r.t. h: L=convolve(h,h) (length 2N-1), pad to Lp=[0,L,0]; c_k=(2*Lp_k+Lp_{k-1}+Lp_{k+1})/3 for k=1..2N-1; dN2/dh_i = 2*sum_k c_k*h_{k-i} over valid indices (implement as a correlation and VERIFY numerically against finite differences on a random N=20 vector); dInf/dh_i = 2*h_{kmax-i} at kmax=argmax(L) (zero other i; if ties, average); dR/dh = (dN2*s^2*inf - N2*(2*s*inf + s^2*dInf/dh))/(s^2*inf)^2 with s=sum h. Then loop: scipy.optimize.minimize(L-BFGS-B, jac=True, bounds=[(0,None)]) maximizing -R from current best; after each solve, perturb current best by 1% relative multiplicative noise on a random half of entries and re-solve; keep best true R. When time remains, upsample current best to N=4000 and continue the same loop until the deadline (leave 1 s margin). Return the highest-R array.
experiments.prediction: R rises to at least 0.825 (target 0.84-0.86), with f*f max still near 0.27 of the support; the fraction of knots within 1% of the max increases, confirming the peaked-g local optimum was unfinished.

experiments.hypothesis: R = ||g||_2^2/(||g||_1||g||_inf) with g=f*f is largest when g is box-like; p0002's g is steeply peaked, so a local optimum may be trapping the peak. Optimizing a soft-inf (log-sum-exp) denominator with small beta rewards flatter, wider g and, with beta annealed to infinity, should land on a flatter-peaked solution with higher true R.
experiments.change: Start from p0002's profile resampled to N=1500. Define R_beta = N2/(s^2 * sbeta) with sbeta = m + log(sum(exp(beta*(L-m))))/beta, m=max(L), using a numerically safe logsumexp (subtract m, guard beta*(L-m) overflow). Gradient identical to the exact-gradient routine but with dInf replaced by 2*sum_k w_k*h_{k-i}, w_k=exp(beta*(L_k-m))/sum_j exp(beta*(L_j-m)). Anneal beta = 5, 20, 80, 320, 1280, 5120, then use the true inf: at each beta run up to 300 L-BFGS-B iterations (bounds [(0,None)]) warm-starting from the previous stage, and after every stage evaluate the TRUE R and record it if it beats the best seen. Return the best-true-R array at the deadline.
experiments.prediction: The fraction of f*f knots within 1% of its maximum rises from 8.2% to >=15% during small beta and true R reaches >=0.815; if R stalls at 0.812 the peaked f*f is genuinely optimal and the plateau route is refuted.

experiments.hypothesis: p0002's basin was found by one seeded random search; a coarse, massively multistarted free-form search (cheap at N=128, exact gradient) may reveal that the asymmetric landscape contains other basins at or above 0.812 that p0002's single run never visited.
experiments.change: Keep start as fallback. Build 40 coarse seeds at N=128: (a) 20 asymmetric parametric profiles h_i=exp(-(|x_i-c|/w)^p)*x_i^a with c,w,p,a drawn log-uniformly (c in [0.15,0.6], w in [0.05,0.6], p in [1,4], a in [0,3]); (b) 20 smoothed random log-uniform arrays (values 10^U(-1,1) convolved with a width-5 box, clipped at 0, mass-normalized). Run exact-gradient L-BFGS-B (same gradient code as the gradient experiment) for 200 iterations on each seed on true R, spending roughly 2-3 s total. Keep the 3 best; upsample the best to N=1200 and continue exact-gradient L-BFGS-B plus random block perturbations until the deadline, returning the best. Also print the per-seed coarse scores.
experiments.prediction: Most coarse seeds land in the symmetric ~0.72 basin or in asymmetric ones scoring 0.78-0.81; the multistart beats 0.812 only if a distinct better basin exists. Whatever the outcome, the printed coarse->refined map tells us whether to keep investing in p0002's basin or this multistart line.

info.open_why: p0002 is the best program and the base for all new experiments; F5/F6 describe the asymmetry mechanism I want to exploit, and p0007 shows a degenerate high-asymmetry shape worth understanding.

plan.analysis: p0009's soft-inf relaxation gave +0.043 with only 4.2 s of 20 s used and stopped at N=1500. The clear bets: (1) spend the whole budget by re-annealing beta at progressively higher resolution and cycling beta; (2) test whether p0009's basin is the best by smoothing-perturbed multistarts re-annealed cheaply; (3) test the theory motivating F7/F12 — that a near-box f*f is optimal — by explicitly fitting f*f to a flat-top target via nonneg least squares and then polishing true R. Bets are spread: refine the winning relaxation, probe basin robustness, and test a structurally different target-driven construction.

experiments.hypothesis: p0009 stopped at N=1500 after 4.2 s with beta capped at 5120; the flat-top still has room to sharpen and the discretization is coarse, so re-annealing beta (5→2e4, then a down/up cycle) at increasing N will find a better flat-top and raise true R.
experiments.change: Load start (p0009's output). Loop over N in [1500, 2400, 4000]: resample current best by linear interpolation to N, then run the existing log-sum-exp soft-inf L-BFGS-B ladder with betas [20, 80, 320, 1280, 5120, 20000, 5120, 20000] (cycling down to 5120 and back up once per resolution), warm-starting each stage from the previous result, maxiter 400. After every stage evaluate true R with _R and keep the best-true-R array (and print it). Continue until 0.9*budget_seconds of CPU time, then do a final exact-gradient L-BFGS-B polish (maxiter 300) of the best array and return it. Ensure bestR/consider initialization is before first use.
experiments.prediction: R reaches ≥ 0.87 (target 0.88-0.90); the 1%-of-max share of f*f knots rises above 40% and ||f*f||_inf stays near 0.93; the run uses ≥ 15 s.

experiments.hypothesis: p0009 may be a local optimum of the box-like basin; smoothing-perturbed restarts (which preserve mass and remove fine spikes in f) re-annealed cheaply from low beta can reach a different, flatter-top basin, as F7's mechanism suggests larger flat regions exist.
experiments.change: From p0009's array, build 8 seeds at its N=1500: convolve h with a normalized Gaussian kernel of sigma in {0.5,1,2,3,4,6,8,12} steps (edge-truncated, mass-renormalized), plus one seed that is the reversed array and one the original. For each seed run the soft-inf ladder beta=[5,20,80,320,1280,5120] with maxiter 120 (cheap ~1.2 s each), record true R for each. Take the top-2 seeds and run the full ladder (beta up to 20000, maxiter 400) with cycling until 0.9*budget CPU, keeping best true R. Print per-seed scores. Guard bestR initialization.
experiments.prediction: Smoothing sigmas ≥ 4 score within ±0.003 of p0009 (basin is robust); if any seed exceeds 0.858 after full anneal, a distinct better basin exists. Either way we learn whether p0009's plateau is a wide basin or a lucky point.

experiments.hypothesis: R is maximized when f*f is box-like; instead of relaxing the inf penalty, directly construct h whose autoconvolution approximates a flat-top trapezoid g_T, then polish true R — this tests whether a genuinely boxy f*f is attainable from a step function and whether that beats 0.855.
experiments.change: Build target g_T on 2N-1 knots: trapezoid with plateau fraction q in {0.2,0.3,0.4} of the support and linear ramps, mass-normalized so sum g_T = 1. For each q, initialize h from p0009's array resampled to N=1000 (fallback ones), and minimize F(h) = ||conv(h,h)/sum(h)^2 - g_T||^2 via L-BFGS-B with bounds [0,None] and analytic gradient (dF/dh using the same convolution-correlation identity as _R_and_grad, precomputed target residual), maxiter 500, 2 s per q. Then take each fitted h, normalize, and run exact-gradient L-BFGS-B on true R (maxiter 300), plus the annealed soft-inf ladder if >4 s remain. Return best true R, and keep p0009 as fallback. Print fit residuals and R values.
experiments.prediction: Best fit gives ||normalized f*f - g_T|| small for q≈0.3 and R after polish in 0.86-0.90 if a near-box f*f is achievable; if fits stall at large residual and R ≤ 0.855, it confirms p0009's f*f shape is near the attainable optimum and points back to the relaxation line.

info.open_why: p0009 is the best program and its full code/annealing schedule plus F7/F12 tell me how to extend the soft-inf idea; p0008 and F8/F5 show the competing asymmetric-basin direction and what gradient-only refinement achieved, so I can pick one refinement and one genuinely different bet.
